stories.title: 📜 4 Macabeos 1
summaryBullets: El libro comienza como un discurso filosófico sobre la supremacía de la razón devota sobre las pasiones (1:1–12).
Se explica que la razón es la mente guiada por la Ley, la cual permite dominar deseos como la codicia, la ira y el miedo (1:13–2:14).
crossRefs: Proverbios 16:32 — Dominar el espíritu es mejor que conquistar una ciudad.
Daniel 1:8 — Daniel rechaza contaminarse con la comida.
Romanos 7:22–23 — La ley de Dios contra la ley del pecado.

stories.title: 📜 4 Macabeos 3
summaryBullets: But this argument is entirely ridiculous, for it is evident that reason rules not over its own passions but over those of the body. (3:1).
No one of us can eradicate that kind of desire, but reason can provide a way for us not to be enslaved by desire. (3:2).
No one of you can eradicate anger from the mind, but reason can help to deal with anger. (3:3).
No one of us can eradicate malice, but reason can fight at our side so that we are not overcome by malice. (3:4).
For reason does not uproot the passions but is their antagonist. (3:5).
Now this can be explained more clearly by the story of King David’s thirst. (3:6).
David had been attacking the Philistines all day long and together with the soldiers of his nation had killed many of them. (3:7).
Then when evening fell, he came, sweating and quite exhausted, to the royal tent, around which the whole army of our ancestors had encamped. (3:8).
Now all the rest were at dinner, (3:9).
but the king was extremely thirsty, and though springs were plentiful there, he could not satisfy his thirst from them. (3:10).
But a certain irrational desire for the water in the enemy’s territory tormented and inflamed him, undid and consumed him. (3:11).

When his guards complained bitterly because of the king’s craving, two staunch young soldiers, respecting the king’s desire, armed themselves fully and taking a pitcher climbed over the enemy’s ramparts. (3:12).
Eluding the sentinels at the gates, they went searching throughout the enemy camp (3:13).
and found the spring and from it boldly brought the king a drink. (3:14).
But David, though he was burning with thirst, considered it an altogether fearful danger to his soul to drink what was regarded as equivalent to blood. (3:15).
Therefore, opposing reason to desire, he poured out the drink as an offering to God. (3:16).
For the temperate mind can conquer the drives of the passions and quench the flames of frenzied desires; (3:17).
it can overthrow bodily agonies even when they are extreme and by nobility of reason spurn all domination by the passions. (3:18).
The present occasion now invites us to a narrative demonstration of temperate reason. (3:19).

At a time when our ancestors were enjoying profound peace because of their observance of the law and were prospering, so that even Seleucus Nicanor, king of Asia, had both appropriated money to them for the temple service and recognized their way of life— (3:20).
just at that time certain persons attempted a revolution against the public harmony and caused many and various disasters. (3:21).

stories.title: 📜 4 Macabeos 5
summaryBullets: The tyrant Antiochus, sitting in state with his counselors on a certain high place and with his armed soldiers standing around him, (5:1).
ordered the guards to seize each and every Hebrew and to compel them to eat pork and food sacrificed to idols. (5:2).
If any were not willing to eat defiling food, they were to be broken on the wheel and killed. (5:3).

When many persons had been rounded up, one man, Eleazar by name, leader of the flock, was brought before the king. He was a man of priestly family, learned in the law, advanced in age, and known to many in the tyrant’s court because of his long career. (5:4).
When Antiochus saw him he said, (5:5).
“Before I begin to torture you, old man, I would advise you to save yourself by eating pork, (5:6).
for I respect your age and your gray hairs. Although you have had them for so long a time, it does not seem to me that you are a philosopher when you observe the religion of the Jews. (5:7).
When nature has granted it to us, why should you abhor eating the very excellent meat of this animal? (5:8).
It is senseless not to enjoy delicious things that are not shameful and wrong to spurn the gifts of nature. (5:9).
It seems to me that you will do something even more senseless if, by holding a vain opinion concerning the truth, you continue to despise me to your own hurt. (5:10).
Will you not awaken from your foolish philosophy, dispel the emptiness of your reasonings, adopt a mind appropriate to your years, philosophize according to the truth of what is beneficial, (5:11).
and have compassion on your old age by honoring my humane advice? (5:12).
For consider this: if there is some power watching over this religion of yours, it will excuse you from any transgression that arises out of compulsion.” (5:13).
When the tyrant urged him in this fashion to eat meat unlawfully, Eleazar asked to have a word. (5:14).
When he had received permission to speak, he began to address the people as follows: (5:15).
“We, O Antiochus, who have been persuaded to govern our lives by the divine law think that there is no compulsion more powerful than our obedience to the law. (5:16).
Therefore we consider that we should not transgress it in any respect. (5:17).
Even if, as you suppose, our law were not truly divine and we had wrongly held it to be divine, not even so would it be right for us to invalidate our reputation for piety. (5:18).
Therefore do not suppose that it would be a petty sin if we were to eat defiling food; (5:19).
to transgress the law in matters either small or great is of equal seriousness, (5:20).
for in either case the law is equally despised. (5:21).
You scoff at our philosophy as though living by it were irrational, (5:22).
but it teaches us self-control, so that we master all pleasures and desires, and it also trains us in courage, so that we endure any suffering willingly; (5:23).
it instructs us in justice, so that in all our dealings we give what is due; and it teaches us piety, so that with proper reverence we worship the only living God. (5:24).

“Therefore we do not eat defiling food, for since we believe that the law was established by God, we know that the Creator of the world in giving us the law has shown sympathy toward us in accordance with nature. (5:25).
He has permitted us to eat what will be most suitable for our lives, but he has forbidden us to eat meats that would be contrary to this. (5:26).
It would be tyrannical for you to compel us not only to transgress the law but also to eat in such a way that you may deride us for eating defiling foods, which are most hateful to us. (5:27).
But you shall have no such occasion to laugh at me, (5:28).
nor will I transgress the sacred oaths of my ancestors concerning the keeping of the law, (5:29).
not even if you gouge out my eyes and burn my entrails. (5:30).
I am not so old and cowardly as not to be young in reason on behalf of piety. (5:31).
Therefore get your torture wheels ready and fan the fire more vehemently! (5:32).
I do not so pity my old age as to overthrow the ancestral law by my own act. (5:33).
I will not play false to you, O law that trained me, nor will I renounce you, beloved self-control. (5:34).
I will not put you to shame, philosophical reason, nor will I reject you, honored priesthood and knowledge of the law. (5:35).
You, O king, shall not defile the honorable mouth of my old age nor my long life lived lawfully. (5:36).
My ancestors will receive me as pure, as one who does not fear your violence even to death. (5:37).
You will tyrannize the ungodly, but you shall not dominate my reasonings on behalf of piety, either by words or through deeds.” (5:38).

stories.title: 📜 4 Macabeos 7
summaryBullets: For like a most skillful pilot, the reason of our father Eleazar steered the ship of piety over the sea of the passions, (7:1).
and though buffeted by the stormings of the tyrant and overwhelmed by the mighty waves of tortures, (7:2).
in no way did he turn the rudder of piety until he sailed into the haven of immortal victory. (7:3).

No city besieged with many ingenious war machines has ever held out as did that most holy man. Although his sacred life was consumed by tortures and racks, he conquered the besiegers because reason was shielding his piety. (7:4).
For in setting his mind firm like a jutting cliff, our father Eleazar broke the maddening waves of the passions. (7:5).
O priest, worthy of the priesthood, you neither defiled your sacred teeth nor profaned your stomach, which had room only for reverence and purity, by eating defiling foods. (7:6).
O man in harmony with the law and philosopher of divine life! (7:7).
Such should be those who are administrators of the law, shielding it with their own blood and noble sweat in sufferings even to death. (7:8).

You, father, validated our obedience to the law through your endurance unto glory, and you did not abandon the holiness that you praised, but by your deeds you made your words of divine philosophy credible. (7:9).
O aged man, more powerful than tortures; O elder, fiercer than fire; O supreme king over the passions, Eleazar! (7:10).
For just as our father Aaron, armed with the censer, ran through the multitude of the people and conquered the fiery angel, (7:11).
so the descendant of Aaron, Eleazar, though being consumed by the fire, remained unmoved in his reason. (7:12).
Most amazing, indeed, though he was an old man, his body no longer tense and firm, his muscles flabby, his sinews feeble, he became young again (7:13).
in spirit through reason, and by reason like that of Isaac he rendered the many-headed rack ineffective. (7:14).
O man of blessed age and of venerable gray hair and of law-abiding life, whom the faithful seal of death has perfected! (7:15).
If, therefore, because of piety an aged man despised tortures even to death, most certainly pious reason is governor of the passions. (7:16).
Some perhaps might say, “Not all have full command of their passions, because not all have prudent reason.” (7:17).
But as many as attend to piety with a whole heart, these alone are able to control the passions of the flesh, (7:18).
since they believe that they, like our patriarchs Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, do not die to God but live to God. (7:19).
No contradiction therefore arises when some persons appear to be dominated by their passions because of the weakness of their reason. (7:20).
What person who lives as a philosopher by the whole rule of philosophy and trusts in God (7:21).
and knows that it is blessed to endure any suffering for the sake of virtue would not be able to overcome the passions through godliness? (7:22).
For only the wise and courageous are masters of their passions. (7:23).

stories.title: 📜 4 Macabeos 9
summaryBullets: “Why do you delay, O tyrant? For we are ready to die rather than transgress our ancestral commandments; (9:1).
we are obviously putting our forebears to shame unless we should practice ready obedience to the law and to Moses our counselor. (9:2).
Tyrant and counselor of lawlessness, in your hatred for us do not pity us more than we pity ourselves. (9:3).
For we consider this pity of yours, which ensures our safety through transgression of the law, to be more grievous than death itself. (9:4).
You are trying to terrify us by threatening us with death by torture, as though a short time ago you learned nothing from Eleazar. (9:5).

And if, on account of piety, the aged men of the Hebrews fulfilled their pious duty while enduring torture, it would be even more fitting that we young men should die despising your coercive tortures, which our aged instructor also overcame. (9:6).
Therefore, tyrant, put us to the test, and if you take our lives because of our piety, do not suppose that you can injure us by torturing us. (9:7).
For we, through this severe suffering and endurance, shall have the prizes of virtue and shall be with God, on whose account we suffer; (9:8).
but you, because of your bloodthirstiness toward us, will deservedly undergo from the divine justice eternal torment by fire.” (9:9).
When they had said these things, the tyrant was not only indignant, as at those who are disobedient, but also infuriated, as at those who are ungrateful. (9:10).
Then at his command the guards brought forward the eldest, and having torn off his tunic, they bound his hands and arms with straps on each side. (9:11).
When they had worn themselves out beating him with scourges, without accomplishing anything, they placed him upon the wheel. (9:12).
When the noble youth was stretched out around this, his limbs were dislocated, (9:13).
and with every member disjointed he denounced the tyrant, saying, (9:14).

“Most abominable tyrant, enemy of heavenly justice, savage of mind, you are mangling me in this manner not because I am a murderer or as one who acts impiously but because I protect the divine law.” (9:15).
And when the guards said, “Agree to eat so that you may be released from the tortures,” (9:16).
he replied, “You abominable lackeys, your wheel is not so powerful as to strangle my reason. Cut my limbs, burn my flesh, and twist my joints; (9:17).
through all these tortures I will convince you that children of the Hebrews alone are invincible when virtue is at stake.” (9:18).
While he was saying these things, they spread fire under him, and while fanning the flames they tightened the wheel further. (9:19).
The wheel was completely smeared with blood, and the heap of coals was being quenched by the drippings of gore, and pieces of flesh were falling off the axles of the machine. (9:20).
Although the ligaments joining his bones were already severed, the courageous youth, worthy of Abraham, did not groan, (9:21).
but as though transformed by fire into immortality he nobly endured the rackings. (9:22).
“Imitate me, brothers,” he said. “Do not leave your post in my struggle or renounce our courageous family ties. (9:23).
Fight the sacred and noble battle for piety. Thereby the just Providence of our ancestors may become merciful to our nation and take vengeance on the accursed tyrant.” (9:24).
When he had said this, the devout youth broke the thread of life. (9:25).

While all were marveling at his courageous spirit, the guards brought forward the next eldest, and after fitting themselves with iron gauntlets having sharp hooks, they bound him to the torture machine and catapult. (9:26).
Before torturing him, they inquired if he were willing to eat, and they heard his noble decision. (9:27).
These leopard-like beasts tore out his sinews with the iron hands, flayed all his flesh up to his chin, and tore away his scalp. But he steadfastly endured this agony and said, (9:28).
“How sweet is any kind of death for our ancestral piety!” (9:29).

To the tyrant he said, “Do you not think, you most savage tyrant, that you are being tortured more than I, as you see the arrogant design of your tyranny being defeated by our endurance for the sake of piety? (9:30).
I lighten my pain by the joys that come from virtue, (9:31).
but you suffer torture by the threats that come from impiety. You will not escape, you most abominable tyrant, the penalties of the divine wrath.” (9:32).

stories.title: 📜 4 Macabeos 10
summaryBullets: When he, too, had endured a glorious death, the third was brought forward, and many repeatedly urged him to save himself by tasting the meat. (10:1).
But he shouted, “Do you not know that the same father begot me as well as those who died and the same mother bore me and that I was brought up on the same teachings? (10:2).
I do not renounce the noble kinship that binds me to my brothers.” (10:3).
Enraged by the man’s boldness, they disjointed his hands and feet with their instruments, dismembering him by prying his limbs from their sockets, (10:5).
and breaking his fingers and arms and legs and elbows. (10:6).
Since they were unable in any way to break his spirit, they abandoned the instruments and scalped him with their fingernails in a Scythian fashion. (10:7).
They immediately brought him to the wheel, and while his vertebrae were being dislocated by this, he saw his own flesh torn all around and drops of blood flowing from his entrails. (10:8).
When he was about to die, he said, (10:9).
“We, most abominable tyrant, are suffering because of our godly training and virtue, (10:10).
but you, because of your impiety and bloodthirstiness, will undergo unceasing torments.” (10:11).
When he, too, had died in a manner worthy of his brothers, they dragged forward the fourth, saying, (10:12).
“As for you, do not give way to the same insanity as your brothers, but obey the king and save yourself.” (10:13).
But he said to them, “You do not have a fire hot enough to make me play the coward. (10:14).
No, by the blessed death of my brothers, by the eternal destruction of the tyrant, and by the everlasting life of the pious, I will not renounce our noble family ties. (10:15).
Contrive tortures, tyrant, so that you may learn from them that I am a brother to those who have just now been tortured.” (10:16).
When he heard this, the bloodthirsty, murderous, and utterly abominable Antiochus gave orders to cut out his tongue. (10:17).
But he said, “Even if you remove my organ of speech, God hears also those who are mute. (10:18).
See, here is my tongue; cut it off, for in spite of this you will not make our reason speechless. (10:19).
Gladly, for the sake of God, we let our bodily members be mutilated. (10:20).
God will visit you swiftly, for you are cutting out a tongue that has been melodious with divine hymns.” (10:21).

stories.title: 📜 4 Macabeos 11
summaryBullets: When he, too, died, after being cruelly tortured, the fifth leaped up, saying, (11:1).
“I will not refuse, tyrant, to be tortured for the sake of virtue. (11:2).
I have come of my own accord so that by murdering me you will incur punishment from the heavenly justice for even more crimes. (11:3).
Hater of virtue, hater of humankind, for what act of ours are you destroying us in this way? (11:4).
Is it because we revere the Creator of all things and live according to his virtuous law? (11:5).
But these deeds deserve honors, not tortures.” (11:6).
While he was saying these things, the guards bound him and dragged him to the catapult; (11:9).

they tied him to it on his knees, and fitting iron clamps on them, they twisted his back around the wedge on the wheel, so that he was completely curled back like a scorpion, and all his members were disjointed. (11:10).
In this condition, gasping for breath and in anguish of body, (11:11).
he said, “Tyrant, they are splendid favors that you grant us against your will, because through these noble sufferings you give us an opportunity to show our endurance for the law.” (11:12).
When he, too, had died, the sixth, a mere boy, was led forward. When the tyrant inquired whether he was willing to eat and be released, he said, (11:13).
“I am younger in age than my brothers, but I am their equal in mind. (11:14).
Since to this end we were born and bred, we ought likewise to die for the same principles. (11:15).
So if you intend to torture me for not eating defiling foods, go on torturing!” (11:16).
When he had said this, they led him to the wheel. (11:17).
He was carefully stretched tight upon it, his back was broken, and he was roasted from underneath. (11:18).
To his back they applied sharp spits that had been heated in the fire and pierced his ribs so that his entrails were burned through. (11:19).

While being tortured he said, “O contest befitting holiness, in which so many of us brothers have been summoned to an arena of sufferings for the sake of piety and in which we have not been defeated! (11:20).
For pious knowledge, O tyrant, is invincible. (11:21).
I also, equipped with nobility, will die with my brothers, (11:22).
and I myself will bring a great avenger upon you, you inventor of tortures and enemy of those who are truly pious. (11:23).
We six boys have overthrown your tyranny. (11:24).
Since you have not been able to persuade us to change our mind or to force us to eat defiling foods, is not this your downfall? (11:25).
Your fire is cold to us, and the catapults painless, and your violence powerless. (11:26).
For it is not the guards of the tyrant but those of the divine law that are set over us; therefore we hold fast to invincible reason.” (11:27).

stories.title: 📜 4 Macabeos 12
summaryBullets: When he, too, thrown into the caldron, had died a blessed death, the seventh and youngest of all came forward. (12:1).

Even though the tyrant had been vehemently reproached by the brothers, he felt strong compassion for this child when he saw that he was already in fetters. He summoned him to come nearer and tried to persuade him, saying, (12:2).
“You see the result of your brothers’ stupidity, for they died in torments because of their disobedience. (12:3).
You, too, if you do not obey, will be miserably tortured and die before your time, (12:4).
but if you yield to persuasion you will be my friend and a leader in the government of the kingdom.” (12:5).

When he had thus appealed to him, he sent for the boy’s mother to show compassion on her who had been bereaved of so many sons and to influence her to persuade the surviving son to obey and save himself. (12:6).
But after his mother had exhorted him in the Hebrew language, as we shall tell a little later, (12:7).
he said, “Let me loose, let me speak to the king and to all his Friends who are with him.” (12:8).
Extremely pleased by the boy’s declaration, they freed him at once. (12:9).
Running to the nearest of the braziers, (12:10).

he said, “You profane tyrant, most impious of all the wicked, since you have received good things and also your kingdom from God, were you not ashamed to murder his servants and torture on the wheel the athletes of piety? (12:11).
Because of this, justice has laid up for you a more intense and eternal fire and tortures, and these throughout all time will never let you go. (12:12).

As a man, were you not ashamed, you most savage beast, to cut out the tongues of people who have feelings like yours and are made of the same elements as you and to maltreat and torture them in this way? (12:13).
Surely they by dying nobly fulfilled their pious duty to God, but you will wail bitterly for having killed without cause the contestants for virtue.” (12:14).
Then because he, too, was about to die, he said, (12:15).
“I do not desert the excellent example of my brothers, (12:16).
and I call on the God of our ancestors to be merciful to our nation, (12:17).
but on you he will take vengeance both in this present life and when you are dead.” (12:18).
After he had uttered these imprecations, he flung himself into the braziers and so ended his life. (12:19).

stories.title: 📜 4 Macabeos 15
summaryBullets: O reason of the children, tyrant over the passions! O piety, more desirable to the mother than her children! (15:1).
Two courses were open to this mother, that of piety and that of preserving her seven sons for a time, as the tyrant had promised. (15:2).
She loved piety more, the piety that preserves them for eternal life according to God’s promise. (15:3).

In what manner might I express the passions of parents who love their children? We impress upon the character of a small child a wondrous likeness both of mind and of form. Especially is this true of mothers, who because of their birth pangs have a deeper sympathy toward their offspring than do the fathers. (15:4).
For to the extent that mothers are of tender spirit and bear more children, so much the more attached are they to their children. (15:5).
The mother of the seven boys, more than any other mother, loved her children. In seven pregnancies she had implanted in herself tender love toward them, (15:6).
and because of the many pains she suffered with each of them she had sympathy for them, (15:7).
yet because of the fear of God she disdained the temporary safety of her children. (15:8).
Not only so, but also because of the nobility of her sons and their ready obedience to the law, she felt a greater tenderness toward them. (15:9).
For they were just and self-controlled and courageous and magnanimous and loved their brothers and their mother so that they obeyed her even to death in keeping the ordinances. (15:10).

Nevertheless, though so many factors influenced the mother to suffer with them out of love for her children, in the case of none of them were the various tortures strong enough to pervert her reason. (15:11).
But each child separately and all of them together the mother urged on to death for piety’s sake. (15:12).
O sacred nature, parental affection, tender love toward offspring, nursing, and indomitable maternal passions! (15:13).
This mother, who saw them tortured and burned one by one, for piety’s sake did not change her attitude. (15:14).
She watched the flesh of her children being consumed by fire, their toes and fingers scattered on the ground, and the flesh of the head to the chin exposed like masks. (15:15).
O mother, tried now by more bitter pains than even the birth pangs you suffered for them! (15:16).
O woman, who alone gave birth to such perfect piety! (15:17).
Neither when the firstborn breathed his last, it did not turn you aside, nor when the second in torments looked at you piteously nor when the third expired, (15:18).
nor did you weep when you looked at the eyes of each one in his tortures gazing boldly at the same agonies and saw in their nostrils the signs of the approach of death. (15:19).

When you saw the flesh of children burned upon the flesh of other children, severed hands upon hands, scalped heads upon heads, and corpses fallen on other corpses, and when you saw the place filled with many spectators because of the children’s torments, you did not shed tears. (15:20).
Neither the melodies of sirens nor the songs of swans attract the attention of their hearers as did the voices of the children in torture calling to their mother. (15:21).
How great and how many torments the mother then suffered as her sons were tortured on the wheel and with the hot irons! (15:22).
But pious reason, giving her heart a man’s courage in the very midst of her passions, strengthened her to disregard, for the time, her parental love. (15:23).
Although she witnessed the destruction of seven children and the ingenious and various rackings, this noble mother disregarded all these because of faith in God. (15:24).
For as in the council chamber of her own soul she saw mighty advocates—nature, family, parental love, and the instruments of torture awaiting her children— (15:25).
this mother held two ballots, one bearing death and the other deliverance for her children. (15:26).
She did not approve the deliverance that would preserve the seven sons for a short time, (15:27).
but as the daughter of God-fearing Abraham she remembered his fortitude. (15:28).
O mother of the nation, vindicator of the law, and defender of piety who carried away the prize of the contest in your heart! (15:29).
O more noble than males in steadfastness and more courageous than men in endurance! (15:30).
Just as Noah’s ark, carrying the world in the universal flood, stoutly endured the waves, (15:31).

so you, O guardian of the law, overwhelmed from every side by the flood of your passions and the violent winds—the torture of your sons—endured nobly and withstood the wintry storms raging on piety’s account. (15:32).

stories.title: 📜 4 Macabeos 18
summaryBullets: O Israelite children, offspring of the seed of Abraham, obey this law and exercise piety in every way, (18:1).
knowing that pious reason is master of the passions, not only of sufferings from within but also of those from without. (18:2).
Therefore those who gave over their bodies in suffering for the sake of piety were not only admired by mortals but also were deemed worthy to share in a divine inheritance. (18:3).
Because of them the nation gained peace, and by reviving observance of the law in the homeland they ravaged the enemy. (18:4).

The tyrant Antiochus was both punished on earth and is being chastised after his death. Since in no way whatever was he able to compel the Israelites to adopt foreign ways and to abandon their ancestral customs, he left Jerusalem and marched against the Persians. (18:5).
The mother of seven sons expressed also these principles to her children: (18:6).
“I was a pure virgin and did not go outside my father’s house, but I guarded the rib from which woman was made. (18:7).
No seducer corrupted me on a desert plain, nor did the destroyer, the deceitful serpent, defile the purity of my virginity. (18:8).

In the time of my maturity I remained with my husband, and when these sons had grown up their father died. A fortunate man was he, who lived out his life with good children and did not have the grief of bereavement. (18:9).
While he was still with you, he taught you the Law and the Prophets. (18:10).
He read to you about Abel slain by Cain and Isaac who was offered as a burnt offering and about Joseph in prison. (18:11).
He told you of the zeal of Phinehas, and he taught you about Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael in the fire. (18:12).
He praised Daniel in the den of the lions and blessed him. (18:13).
He reminded you of the scripture of Isaiah, which says, ‘Even though you go through the fire, the flame shall not consume you.’ (18:14).
He sang to you songs of the psalmist David, who said, ‘Many are the afflictions of the righteous.’ (18:15).
He recounted to you Solomon’s proverb, ‘There is a tree of life for those who do his will.’ (18:16).
He confirmed the query of Ezekiel, ‘Shall these dry bones live?’ (18:17).
For he did not forget to teach you the song that Moses taught, which says, (18:18).
‘I kill, and I make alive; this is your life and the length of your days.’ ” (18:19).

O bitter was that day—and yet not bitter—when that bitter tyrant of the Greeks quenched fire with fire in his cruel caldrons and in his burning rage brought those seven sons of the daughter of Abraham to the catapult and back again to more tortures, (18:20).
pierced the pupils of their eyes and cut out their tongues, and put them to death with various tortures. (18:21).
For these crimes divine justice pursued and will pursue the accursed tyrant. (18:22).
But the sons of Abraham with their victorious mother are gathered together into the chorus of the fathers and have received pure and immortal souls from God, (18:23).
to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. (18:24).
